title: Token Auth & Rate Limits API
summary: Fix a role check that lets viewers write and a health check stuck behind auth, add ownership rules and an admin audit log with cursor paging, then replace a leaky rate limiter with an exact, fast sliding window.
overview:
You've joined the team behind **Inkwell**, a team wiki. This codebase is its documents API. Every client (the web editor, the CLI, CI bots) calls it with an API token, and each token belongs to a user with one role: `viewer`, `editor` or `admin`.

A request passes through a chain of middleware in `src/app.js`: body parsing, `authenticate` (Bearer token to `req.user`), the per-token `rateLimit`, then the routers. Each route in `src/routes/` declares the minimum role it needs with `requireRole(...)`. Controllers call services in `src/services/`, which work on the in-memory tables in `src/store/memory-store.js`. The limiting algorithm lives on its own in `src/lib/rate-limiter.js`, independent of HTTP.

Start with `README.md`: it documents the roles, every endpoint, the error codes and the rate limit headers, and the tests check exactly that contract. Then read `src/app.js` top to bottom, since in Express the **order** of `app.use` calls is the security model. `demo.js` makes a few calls as different users and prints the results.

phases.title: Who can do what
phases.instructions:
Two reports, one of them urgent:

> **Security (urgent):** *"Vic has a viewer token, and Vic just edited the on-call runbook. Editors can delete documents too, which should be admin-only. Meanwhile Ada, our admin, gets `403 forbidden` when she tries to create a document, and some editors can't even read."*

> **Platform:** *"The load balancer marks every instance unhealthy. `GET /health` returns `401` because the balancer sends no token."*

The intended rules are in `README.md`: roles are ordered `viewer` < `editor` < `admin`, each route's minimum role is in the endpoint table, and `/health` is the only public route. Find the root causes and fix them without weakening authentication for any other route: a missing token must still be `401 unauthenticated` with a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, and a bad one `401 invalid_token`.

**Done when:** all tests in `tests/phase1.test.js` pass.
hints: Try each role against each route (the tests or `node demo.js` do this). Write down which combinations are wrong: is there a pattern in which roles are let through and which are blocked?
`requireRole` is in `src/middleware/require-role.js`. Look at how it decides whether `req.user.role` is high enough. What does `<` do when both sides are strings like `'viewer'` and `'editor'`?

For the health check, read `src/app.js` from top to bottom. Express runs middleware and routes in the order they are registered, and `app.use(authenticate(...))` applies to everything registered after it.

phases.title: Ownership, revocation and the audit log
phases.instructions:
Security signed off on three changes.

**1. Editors only edit their own documents.** `PATCH /docs/:id` by an editor whose id is not the document's `ownerId` is `403 forbidden`, and the document is unchanged. Admins may edit any document. (An unknown id is still `404`.)

**2. Token revocation.** `POST /admin/tokens/:id/revoke` (admin only) revokes a token by its id and returns `200` with the token record **without its `secret`**, including `"revoked": true`. From then on that token is `401 invalid_token`; the user's other tokens keep working. An unknown token id is `404`.

**3. The audit log.** Record an entry for every **write** (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) on any path, whatever its outcome, and for every **refused** request (`401` or `403`), including reads. Successful reads are not recorded. An entry is:

```json
{"id": "aud_000042", "at": "2026-05-04T12:00:01.000Z", "actor": "usr_eli", "role": "editor",
 "method": "PATCH", "path": "/docs/doc_0003", "status": 403, "outcome": "denied"}
```

`at` comes from the app's `clock` at the time of the request. `actor` and `role` are `null` when the request had no valid token. `path` excludes the query string. `outcome` is `denied` for 401 and 403, `success` for other statuses below 400, and `failed` otherwise.

`GET /admin/audit` (admin only) returns `{"data": [entry, ...], "nextCursor": "..." | null}`, **newest first**, with optional query parameters `actor` (exact user id), `outcome`, `limit` (1 to 100, default 50) and `cursor` (the `nextCursor` of the previous page). `nextCursor` is `null` on the last page. Paging must stay correct while new entries are being added: following cursors returns every older entry exactly once. Invalid parameters, including a cursor this endpoint did not issue, are `422 validation_error` naming every bad parameter.

**Done when:** the phase 1 and phase 2 tests pass.
hints: Start with ownership: the controller already passes `req.user` to `updateDoc`. Revocation is a new route in `src/routes/admin.js`, a controller method and a small token service; the store already has `getToken` and `updateToken`.

Recording needs to see the final status code and `req.user`, and must also see requests that `authenticate` rejects. Write a middleware that registers `res.on('finish', ...)` and calls `next()`, and think about **where** in `src/app.js` it has to be mounted to see a 401.

Don't use an offset for the cursor: new entries arrive at the front, so offsets shift. The store gives each entry an increasing `seq`; a cursor that encodes the last `seq` returned (for example base64url of `aud:<seq>`) means "entries older than this one". Validate it on decode, apply the filters while walking backwards, and fetch one extra to know whether there is a next page.

phases.title: A rate limiter you can trust
phases.instructions:
The limiter in `src/lib/rate-limiter.js` counts requests in fixed windows aligned to the clock. Two problems showed up in production:

> *"A scraper sent 600 requests at 11:59:59.5 and another 600 at 12:00:00.5: 1,200 requests in one second on a 600-a-minute token."*

> *"After a burst, clients are told `Retry-After` values that don't match when they actually get through."*

Replace it with an **exact sliding window**, keeping the same interface (`createRateLimiter({limit, windowMs, now})` returning `{hit(key)}`, where `hit` returns `{allowed, limit, remaining, retryAfterMs}`):

- A request at time `t` is allowed when fewer than `limit` **allowed** requests for that key happened in the window `(t - windowMs, t]`: a request made at `s` stops counting at exactly `s + windowMs`.
- **Refused requests do not count**, so a client hammering while blocked is not blocked longer.
- `remaining` is how many more requests would be allowed right now after this one (0 when refused). `retryAfterMs` is 0 when allowed; when refused it is the time until the oldest counted request leaves the window. The HTTP layer already turns it into `Retry-After` in whole seconds, rounded up, at least 1.
- **It must be fast.** Limits can be in the thousands per token. The tests replay 600,000 seeded requests from 20 tokens with a limit of 5,000 per 5 seconds and require all of them to be checked within one second, and every result must match an exact reference. A hit must not scan or copy every request in the window.

Keep the per-token behaviour in the HTTP tests: separate budgets per token, unauthenticated requests never counted, `/health` never limited.

**Done when:** all three phases' tests pass.
hints: First see why the fixed window is wrong: with a 10 s window, 5 requests at 9.5 s and 5 more at 10.5 s are all allowed, though 10 happened within one second. A sliding window has to remember *when* each counted request happened.

The obvious version keeps an array of timestamps per key and does `times = times.filter(t => now - t < windowMs)` on every hit. It is correct but O(limit) per hit, and at 5,000 per window the replay test runs out of time. Timestamps arrive in order: expired ones are always at the front.

Use a queue per key with a moving head: a ring buffer of size `limit` (a `Float64Array` works well) with `head` and `count`. On each hit, advance `head` past expired times, then append if `count < limit`. When full, `retryAfterMs = times[head] + windowMs - now`. Occasionally delete keys whose newest request has expired, so idle tokens don't hold memory forever.

debrief: Why did viewers get write access while admins were refused, and why did the health check need a token? How did you confirm both causes before changing the code?
Where did you mount the audit middleware and why does that position matter? Explain how your cursor stays correct while new entries are being added, compared with offset paging.

Walk through your sliding-window limiter: what does one hit cost in time and memory, why do refused requests not count, and how did you check that the AI's limiter was exact rather than approximately right?
